catalog_quote: [p. 16] 3. Klemtoon. Veelal valt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep, bijv. lóbo, vinger; séli, eten; wawái, kind; sadakála, hagedis; saláwe, losmaken. Is dit het geval dan wordt dit in de spelling niet tot uitdrukking gebracht. Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon altijd, indien de slotvocaal gerekt is, bijv. kakanū, eczeem; malī, herwaarts; kakalā, rood. Ook dit wordt in de spelling niet door een afzonderlijk teken aangeduid. Soms echter valt het accent op de slotsyllabe zonder dat deze een gerekte vocaal bevat, bijv. kakanín, zuur; totoláng, zitten; gagalúm, week; pupuráng, wan; gaglí, mager. Slechts in die gevallen zal dit door middel van een accent aigu worden aangegeven. ... tone_statements.quote: Within SHWNG, tone is found in the Raja Ampat languages Maˈya and Matbat and the Cenderawasih Bay languages Moor, Yerisiam, and Yaur. [...] Traces of former penultimate stress were found in Maˈya, Moor, and Yerisiam. Penul- timate stress is cited as the regular or default pattern in most other SHWNG languages for which descriptions are available: the South Halmahera languages Buli (Maan 1951: 16), Sawai (Whisler and Whisler 1995: 660), and Taba (Bowden 2001: 62); the Cendera- wasih Bay languages Ambai (Silzer 1983: 40), Wandamen (Henning 1991: xviii), and Waropen (Held 1942b: 28); and the Mamberamo language Warembori (Donohue 1999: 7).
tone_statements.locator: p. 95, sec. 5.1 'Introduction' (first sentence) and p. 117, sec. 5.4 'Implications for subgrouping' (second part)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone in Buli; penultimate word stress (per Maan 1951), tone in SHWNG confined to Raja Ampat and Cenderawasih Bay languages.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on printed p.16 (and p.13) of the OAPEN PDF we hold. (2) The classification rests on the only grammar of the language, Maan 1951 (160 pp, KITLV), first-hand though impressionistic; WALS and StressTyp2 independently code Buli the same way (right-edge, ult/penult, long-vowel weight) from the same source, matching our 'weight-hedged, CVV, right edge' record. The hedge ('veelal' penult, 'soms' unmarked-final) is in the source itself, so the 14/20 rule-fit note reflects lexical exceptions Maan explicitly flags, not a misreading. Penul- timate stress is cited as the regular or default pattern in most other SHWNG languages for which descriptions are available: the South Halmahera languages Buli (Maan 1951: 16), Sawai (Whisler and Whisler 1995: 660), and Taba (Bowden 2001: 62); the Cendera- wasih Bay languages Ambai (Silzer 1983: 40), Wandamen (Henning 1991: xviii), and Waropen (Held 1942b: 28); and the Mamberamo language Warembori (Donohue 1999: 7).

sources.note: States that within SHWNG lexical tone is found (only) in the Raja Ampat languages Ma'ya and Matbat and the Cenderawasih Bay languages Moor, Yerisiam and Yaur; Buli is cited (after Maan 1951: 16) as a language with regular/default penultimate stress, taken as a retention of Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress; tone in SHWNG arose independently 4-5 times, never in South Halmahera.
